result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.is_isomorphic()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Check if this graph is isomorphic to another graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L9221-L9349){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.is_isomorphic(other) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Is isomorphic](/assets/graphs/is-isomorphic.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Each side compares graph g with graph h. Left: g is a five-node cycle and h is the same cycle redrawn as a star, so is_isomorphic(h) returns True. Right: h is a triangle with a two-edge tail; it has the same node and edge counts, but its degree-3 node C and degree-1 node E (shown in the accent color) have no match in the cycle, so is_isomorphic(h) returns False." width="100%"} Two graphs are isomorphic if there exists a one-to-one correspondence (bijection) between their nodes that preserves the adjacency relationship. In simpler terms, they have the same structure but possibly different node labels. This implementation does *not* search for such a correspondence. Instead it checks the following necessary conditions: - same directedness - same number of nodes - same number of edges - same degree sequence (for directed graphs, the sorted out-degrees are compared) A `False` result is therefore definitive: the graphs cannot be isomorphic. A `True` result only means no difference was found by these cheap tests; structurally different graphs can still pass (see the last example). Labels, weights, and node or edge attributes are ignored, and so is the current selection. Because the checks are cheap (about the cost of sorting the degrees), this is a fast way to: - rule out most non-matching graphs before running an expensive exact comparison - spot accidental structural changes (e.g. a lost edge) between two versions of a graph - group a collection of graphs into candidate structural classes ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [other]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The `Graph` to compare this graph with. It is not modified. Its node labels and IDs don't need to match this graph's in any way, since only the structure is compared. Passing an object that is not a `Graph` raises an `AttributeError`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if the two graphs agree on all of the conditions above (they may be isomorphic), `False` if they differ on at least one (they are definitely not isomorphic). ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} A true isomorphism between graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ is a bijection $\pi: V_1 \to V_2$ such that $(u, v) \in E_1 \iff (\pi(u), \pi(v)) \in E_2$. Deciding whether such a $\pi$ exists is the graph isomorphism problem, famous for sitting in $\mathsf{NP}$ but not known to be in $\mathsf{P}$ or $\mathsf{NP}\text{-complete}$, and solved in practice by backtracking algorithms like VF2 or Babai's quasi-polynomial procedure. This method instead checks a handful of cheap *invariants* (node count, edge count, degree sequence, directedness) which any isomorphism must preserve. Two graphs that disagree on any invariant are provably non-isomorphic, but agreement is only suggestive: many non-isomorphic graphs share the same degree sequence. Use this as a fast filter before running a full isomorphism check. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Two paths of the same length are isomorphic even though their node labels differ -- what matters is the structure, not the names: ::: {#289c7a11 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g1 = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) ) g2 = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["X", "Y", "Z"]) .add_edges([("X", "Y"), ("Y", "Z")]) ) g1.is_isomorphic(g2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` True ``` ::: ::: A path and a star of the same size have different degree sequences, so they're correctly ruled out: ::: {#04c4b93a .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} path = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_path_graph(n=4) star = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_star_graph(n=4) path.is_isomorphic(star) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` False ``` ::: ::: Directedness is compared too, so an otherwise-identical directed and undirected graph don't count as isomorphic: ::: {#81c7ed8e .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} directed = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_path_graph(n=3) undirected = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_path_graph(n=3) directed.is_isomorphic(undirected) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` False ``` ::: ::: Two complete graphs of the same size are always isomorphic, since every node is interchangeable: ::: {#edaeedf7 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} k4_a = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_full_graph(n=4) k4_b = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_full_graph(n=4) k4_a.is_isomorphic(k4_b) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` True ``` ::: ::: Graphs of different sizes can never be isomorphic: ::: {#66897060 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} g3 = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_cycle_graph(n=3) g4 = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_cycle_graph(n=4) g3.is_isomorphic(g4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` False ``` ::: ::: Because only invariants are compared, a `True` result is not proof. A six-node cycle and two separate triangles both have six nodes, six edges, and every degree equal to `2`, so they pass the check even though one is connected and the other is not: ::: {#c4d207a4 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} hexagon = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_cycle_graph(n=6) two_triangles = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_cycle_graph(n=3).add_cycle_graph(n=3) hexagon.is_isomorphic(two_triangles), hexagon.is_connected(), two_triangles.is_connected() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` (True, True, False) ``` ::: :::
